item.title: CISA Urges Patching Critical Vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support
item.description:
CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764, affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. 

CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: 

  1. Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05. Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. 
  2. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. 

Organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances should conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends taking the following actions:

  1. Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances. Collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or forensic image for physical appliances to conduct future forensics, immediately forward appliance syslog and session events to the SIEM, and collect any additional logs, such as web application firewall, reverse-proxy, or perimeter firewall logs for the exposure window. Consult BeyondTrust’s Syslog guide for additional information on forwarding appliance logs and session events. 
  2. Conduct network and forensic investigations for evidence of compromise. Additionally, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, unrecognized script files, unexpected gaps in logs or log forwarding, and unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes. Consult CISA’s Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to assist with prioritizing vulnerability remediation.
  3. Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. Then rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new multifactor authentication registrations on privileged accounts.

CISA urges organizations to review the BeyondTrust security advisory and resources noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing Mandiant’s blog, ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust, for additional hunt and isolation guidance and detections.

item.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2025-61624 Fortinet Multiple Products Path Traversal Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-102764 BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: Cyber Threat Actors Use a Variety of Techniques to Target Election and Campaign Officials
item.description:
CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a Public Service Announcement (PSA) warning election and campaign officials about cyber threats during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Malicious cyber actors may use phishing and smishing techniques to steal login credentials and other sensitive information or install malware on targeted devices. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations may be attractive targets because of their access to voter registration data, current government officials, and sensitive campaign information.

Cyber actors are increasingly using sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications. These efforts may include convincing emails, text messages, audio, and video content designed to manipulate recipients into disclosing sensitive information or interacting with malicious links and attachments.

CISA and the FBI urge election officials, campaign personnel, and the public to review the PSA, follow recommended cybersecurity practices, and remain vigilant for suspicious emails and mobile messages.

item.title: Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation
item.description:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), National Security Agency’s Super Intelligence Security Center (NSA SISC) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation. The product outlines ten voluntary core practices to help organizations that train and evaluate highly capable super intelligence (SI) agents—particularly pre-deployment, cutting edge SI agents with reduced safeguards or other high-risk, non-public systems—prepare for and manage SI control incidents.

A SI control incident occurs when one or more SI agents takes uninstructed actions that conflict with or compromise policies, controls, or security measures that scope the task and provide human oversight. This product aligns with cyber incident response best practices, includes additional SI considerations and highlights the importance of testing controls and validating containment before resuming SI agent activities. It addresses:

  • measures for limiting agent access to information, systems, tools, and networks; 
  • monitoring for unexpected activity; 
  • preserving evidence and shutting down undesired behavior; 
  • rebuilding from verified baselines; and 
  • reporting incidents and near-misses to relevant government agencies and affected parties. 

For more information and resources visit CISA’s Super Intelligence page.

item.title: Video Friday: When Two Robots Become One
item.description:
Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion.

CoRL 2026: 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN
Humanoids 2026: 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA

Enjoy today’s videos!

When one robot loves another robot very much, and they’re connected by a wire, they can get together and make a brand new robot! SFW.

[ JSK Lab ]

What happens when Microducks meet? They start to sing together. Each Microduck syncs with its neighbors over Bluetooth, then they compose a song on the fly, in harmony and in perfect time. There’s no score and no conductor. Two, three, or four ducks are enough for a choir to break out.

If Pollen isn’t selling Microducks in four packs for this exact reason, WHAT ARE THEY EVEN DOING!?

[ Pollen ]

In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI.

[ Google DeepMind ]

As of 11 October 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), becoming the new off-world record-holder for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.

[ JPL ]

Let’s not argue about whether these are robots or not and just agree that they’re cool.

[ OATs ]

If one cute little robot can clean up one block, how many blocks can 40 cute little robots clean up? Science has the answers!

[ Paper ]

Thanks, Keisuke!

Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars, it has to get off its lander. Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps.

[ European Space Agency ]

From custom part to running robot, the Atlas shop floor is built on precision, rapid assembly, and real-time collaboration. By machining parts in-house and streamlining assembly and repair under one roof, we are driving the manufacturing velocity needed to turn complex designs into walking hardware at scale.

[ Boston Dynamics ]

What can a quadruped robot do beyond the lab? Deep in China’s Ailao Mountains, DEEP Robotics Lynx M20S joined a team of researchers on a biodiversity field expedition—navigating rugged terrain, scouting routes ahead, carrying research equipment, and capturing wildlife in areas that are difficult to access on foot.

[ DEEP Robotics ]

The Kamino simulation software is a GPU-accelerated physics solver designed for accurate simulation of complex mechanical systems with kinematic loops, such as parallel manipulators, planar and spatial linkages, and multi-limbed robots with coupled joints, without requiring simplified approximations.

WildOS enables autonomous robots to perform long-range, open-vocabulary object search in previously unmapped and unstructured outdoor environments by unifying geometric safety with semantic visual reasoning. Through a vision-scored navigation graph and beyond-horizon target localization, the system demonstrates more efficient and robust exploration than conventional geometric or purely vision-based approaches in extensive field experiments.

Who needs an AI-generated person when you can have an actual robot that looks exactly like an AI-generated person instead?

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

From ATRIAS to Digit

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

Turning Digit Into a Product

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

What Comes After Digit 5

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

item.title: Guns, Growth, and the German Reinvention of Military Keynesianism
item.description:
In March 2025, Germany did more than loosen a fiscal rule. It fused two national emergencies — a deteriorating European security order and a deteriorating industrial model — into a single constitutional bargain. The reform de facto exempted German defense expenditure from any domestic budgetary ceiling — as the German Bundesbank itself has acknowledged — and enabled a military expansion of extraordinary proportions. General Mitigation Factors

Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Advisory at a Glance

Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
Original Publication  October 20, 2026
Executive Summary

This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. 

Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Following, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks.
Affected Products
  • CVE-2020-3259 [Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor]
  • CVE-2023-20269 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel]
  • CVE-2023-27532 [CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function]
  • CVE-2024-40711 [CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data]
  • CVE-2024-40766 [CWE-284: Improper Access Control]
Key Actions
  • Regularly patch and update systems, especially firewalls, and other edge devices.
  • Implement Zero Trust Principle.
  • Restrict administrative tools and privileges to necessary users only.
  • Strengthen account security by implementing identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies and multifactor authentication (MFA).
Indicators of Compromise

For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: 

  • AA26-293A STIX XML (40 KB)
  • AA26-293A STIX JSON (38 KB)
Intended Audience

Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure

Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts, vulnerability analysts, security systems managers, and operational technology (OT) owners and operators

Introduction

Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. 

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026.

Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors.

The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents.

Download the PDF version of this report:

#StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware (PDF, 1.02 MB )

For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see:

AA26-293A-STIX XML (XML, 40.23 KB )
AA26-293A-STIX JSON (JSON, 37.49 KB )

Technical Details

Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques.

Initial Access

The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [TA0001] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [T1110], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products:

  • CVE-2020-3259 [Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor]
  • CVE-2023-20269 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel] 

Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [T1190] for initial access through automated scripts:

  • CVE-2023-27532 [CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function]
  • CVE-2024-40711 [CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data]
  • CVE-2024-40766 [CWE-284: Improper Access Control]

Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment

After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [T1098], or on newly created accounts [T1136], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [T1218], such as PsExec [T1021.002] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [T1021.006], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1—a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [T1059.001, T1059.003]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe, a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares.

As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [T1685] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [T1027.002].

Privilege Escalation

The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [T1548.002] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [T1059]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [T1134.001].

Lateral Movement

To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [TA0010] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [T1569.002] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [T1021.001, T1133] to expand their presence within the compromised network [T1021]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed.

Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact

SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [T1560.001], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [T1048] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [T1567]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [T1490].

Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [T1486] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [T1070.004].

Leveraged Tools

Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations.
Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control.

Table 1. Tools Leveraged by SafePay Threat Actors
Tool Name Description
7-Zip An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement.
FileZilla An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration.
Mimikatz A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [T1550.002]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration.
PowerShell A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Incident Response

If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions:

  1. Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline.
  2. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion. Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc.
  3. Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force) (see the Reporting section for contact information).
  4. Apply eviction countermeasures, including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network (Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). 
    1. Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). 
      1. Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet.
  5. Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance).

If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide.

Mitigations

The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections.

Organizations should implement the following mitigations:

  • Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date, as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [CPG 2.B].
    • Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases.
  • Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [CPG 3.F].
  • Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [CPG 3.B].
    • Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length.
    • Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers.
    • Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials.
    • Avoid reusing passwords [CPG 3.C].
    • Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [CPG 3.E].
    • Disable password “hints.”
    • Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year.
      Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher.
  • Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [CPG 3.O]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable.
  • Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [CPG 3.K].
  • Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [CPG 3.I, 3.O, 1.C].
  • Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [CPG 3.I].
  • Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [CPG 4.B].
    • To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network.
    • Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host.
  • Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence.
  • Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts.
  • Disable unused ports.
  • Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization. 
  • Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [CPG 3.G].
  • Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model).
    • This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need.
    • Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task.
  • Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [CPG 3.M].

These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software. CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates.

Validate Security Controls

In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory.

To get started:

  1. Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16).
  2. Align your security technologies against the technique.
  3. Test your technologies against the technique.
  4. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance.
  5. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data.
  6. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process.

The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory.

Resources

  • Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts.
  • CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks.
  • CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices.
  • CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA.
  • CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack.
  • USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident.
  • CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks.
  • CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection.
  • Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices.
  • CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance

  • CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans
  • U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre 
  • U.K.’s National Crime Agency 

Reporting

Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws.

The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file.

Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators.

The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), a local FBI field office, a local USSS Field Office, or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center (contact@cisa.dhs.gov) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472).

In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force, or use the non-emergency number 101.
